transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess… I’m here because I can’t keep my mind on what I’m supposed to be doing anymore. Like at work, I’ll be in the middle of an experiment or on a grant call, and then I’ll notice something tiny—a pump vibration, or a student makes some side comment, or there’s this weird little peak in an old spectrum—and suddenly that’s all I can think about.

And then hours are gone. I mean, sometimes it feels important, like I’ve found some clue everyone else missed, but meanwhile the actual thing people needed from me is just… not done. Safety meetings are terrible for that too, because there are so many noises and little details in the room, and I’ll start following one thread and lose the whole point. It’s gotten bad enough that things are starting to fall apart.
Do you feel like this tendency to get caught up in tiny details is causing you a lot of stress or anxiety?

Yes. It’s stressful because it’s not just, you know, being curious or detail-oriented. I’ll be on a grant call or in a safety meeting, and then I hear a pump vibrating funny, or a student says something offhand, or I remember some strange peak in an old spectrum, and my brain just… leaves. I’m gone chasing that for hours.

And meanwhile the actual experiment, the thing people are waiting on, just doesn’t get done. Then I’m trying to explain why something important fell apart because I got stuck on this tiny thing that felt urgent at the time. It makes me anxious, yes—mostly because I can see it happening and still can’t pull myself back.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting or feeling restless when you're sitting still?

Yes—restless, definitely. Sitting still feels almost… wrong sometimes, like I’m wasting time I don’t have.

I’ll get to the lab before anyone else is even there and I’m rewriting protocols, moving instrument schedules around, emailing collaborators in different countries—because, you know, someone in Germany is already awake, and then Singapore, and then it becomes this whole chain—and I’ll start three analyses at the same time. Not even one after another, all at once.

It’s like if I sit down quietly, I’m missing the one window where I could fix everything. So yes, I fidget, but it’s more than that. I can’t stay put.
Do you find yourself repeating certain actions or rituals over and over?

I’m not sure I’d call them rituals. I mean, I do things more than once sometimes, but usually it’s because I got pulled into whether it was done correctly—like in the lab, there are procedures where you really are supposed to check things.

But “rituals” makes me think of, I don’t know, having to tap a doorway or count tiles or something like that. I don’t think I have that. Unless you mean… like going back over an email three times because one sentence feels wrong, but then that’s more because the wording matters, especially when it’s to a collaborator, and then I start thinking about how they’ll interpret it and whether it sounds too blunt. So… I guess I haven’t really noticed repeated actions in that way.
Do you feel like your work or tasks need to be perfect, or that there will be serious consequences if they are not done perfectly?

I don’t know if I’d say “perfect” exactly. I mean, in my work, sometimes a tiny error really does matter—like if a calibration is off, or a label is wrong, or someone assumes a sample was handled one way when it wasn’t. So I do care about precision.

But serious consequences if it isn’t perfect… I’m not sure. That sounds dramatic, and then again, in a lab, “dramatic” can just mean someone has to redo three days of work because the wrong file got saved. Sorry, I’m getting into the weeds.

I guess I notice when things are imperfect, but I don’t know if it’s this feeling that everything has to be perfect or else something terrible will happen. I haven’t really thought about it that way.
Do you feel anxious or uneasy when you're unable to complete a task exactly as you envisioned it?

I’m not sure. I mean… “as I envisioned it” is tricky, because half the time the way I envisioned it changes while I’m doing it.

Like I’ll start with one plan for a report or an experiment setup, and then I’ll notice something else that could be improved, and then suddenly the original task isn’t even the same task anymore. So if I can’t finish it exactly the way I pictured it at first, I don’t know that I feel anxious, exactly. Maybe irritated? Or like I need to keep thinking about it.

But then again, sometimes you have to just submit the thing because there’s a deadline, and everyone acts like that’s normal, which—sorry, this reminds me of this one collaborator who would send comments at the absolute last second and then disappear for two days. So I don’t know. I haven’t really noticed a specific uneasy feeling tied to it not matching my original vision.
Do you feel a strong need to control or organize your environment, even when it's not necessarily required?

Yes—well, not control like everything has to be color-coded at home or anything. But at work, if things feel loose, I have this almost physical need to get in there and straighten it out.

I’ll get to the lab before anyone else is even there, and I’ll start rewriting protocols, moving instrument schedules around, emailing collaborators in different countries because they’re awake when we’re not, and then I’ll open three new analyses because suddenly it seems obvious how to fix all of it. And it’s not always required, exactly. It’s more like… if I don’t do it right then, I’m wasting the chance to get everything lined up.

Sorry, that probably sounds more intense than “organizing my environment,” but yes, I guess I do.
Do you feel a strong urge to make things symmetrical or exact in your daily life?

Symmetrical or exact… not really in the sense of, like, the mug has to be lined up with the edge of the table or I can’t leave the room.

I mean, I notice if something is off-center, especially on a graph or a slide, because then it looks sloppy and people start commenting on the wrong thing instead of the data. Actually, that happened once in a presentation where someone spent ten minutes talking about axis labels instead of the result, which was maddening because—sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

In daily life, I don’t think I have a strong urge for symmetry. Exactness, maybe in work things, but not like arranging objects or needing things even. I haven’t noticed that.
Do you think your tendency to get caught up in details is because you want everything to be just right, or because you have trouble ignoring small things that catch your attention?

I think it’s more the second one. I don’t know that it’s about wanting everything to be “just right” in some tidy, perfect way.

It’s more like small things grab me and then I can’t let them go. That’s actually part of why I came in. I can’t keep my mind on the actual experiment anymore. I’ll be on a grant call or in a safety meeting, and I’ll notice the vibration in a pump, or one comment a student makes off to the side, or some weird peak in an old spectrum, and then suddenly that’s the whole thing. I’m chasing that for hours.

And meanwhile the thing everyone actually needed from me—the report, the meeting decision, whatever—just kind of falls apart. I don’t mean to do it. It just feels like my attention gets pulled sideways.
Do you feel like you're getting caught up in details because you're trying to make sure everything is correct, or because you just can't help but notice them?

It’s more that I can’t help noticing them. I mean, yes, I like things to be correct, obviously—if the data are wrong, that’s a problem—but that’s not really what it feels like.

It’s like my attention gets hooked. I’ll be in the middle of a grant call or a safety meeting, and then I hear a pump vibrating differently, or a student says something off to the side, or I remember some odd peak in an old spectrum, and suddenly that’s where I am. I’ll follow it for hours, even when the actual experiment or the decision people needed from me is just… falling apart.

And then later I realize I never got back to the main thing. It’s frustrating because in the moment it feels urgent, like I have to chase it right then.
Do you think you get caught up in details because you're afraid of missing something important or making a mistake?

Maybe a little, but it doesn’t feel like fear exactly. It’s not like I’m sitting there thinking, “If I miss this, something terrible will happen.” It’s more immediate than that.

I’ll be in the middle of the actual thing I’m supposed to be doing—the grant call, the safety meeting, the experiment—and then some tiny thing pulls me. A pump sounds different, or someone mutters something at the side of the room, or I remember that weird peak from an old spectrum, and suddenly I’m off after it. Hours can go by.

And the stupid part is, the important thing was probably the meeting or the experiment in front of me, but by then I’ve let that fall apart. So… not exactly afraid of mistakes. More like I can’t not follow the detail once it catches me.
Do you think your tendency to get caught up in details is more about making sure everything is correct or about being unable to ignore the details that catch your attention?

It’s definitely more that I can’t ignore them. I mean, I care about being correct, of course, but that’s not really what’s happening.

It’s like—I’ll be trying to focus on the actual experiment, and then something small catches me. A pump vibration, or some comment a student makes off to the side, or I suddenly remember an odd peak in an old spectrum, and then I’m gone. I’ll chase that for hours.

And then the grant call, or the safety meeting, or whatever people actually needed from me just falls apart. That’s why I came in, honestly. I can’t keep my mind on the main thing anymore.
Do you think you would be able to focus on the main task if the small details that catch your attention were somehow resolved or eliminated?

I’d like to think so, but honestly I don’t know. Because it isn’t just one detail to remove, you know? If the pump vibration were fixed, then it would be the student whispering something, or I’d suddenly remember that old spectrum with the strange peak—sorry, that one still bothers me because I never really figured out if it was contamination or the detector acting up.

But yes, I mean… if somehow none of those things grabbed me, maybe I could stay with the actual experiment. That’s the whole problem. I came in because I can’t keep my mind on the main task anymore. I’ll be on a grant call or in a safety meeting and then one small thing hooks me, and I’m off chasing it for hours while the thing people actually needed from me falls apart.
Do you think you could consider a task complete even if it's not done exactly as you had envisioned it?

I’m not sure. I think sometimes I can, if it’s something small or if no one is going to look too closely at it.

But “as I envisioned it” is tricky, because usually the thing changes while I’m doing it. Like with an experiment, the picture in my head at the start is never the thing at the end, because then there’s some odd reading or someone asks a question, and suddenly the whole shape of it is different. I don’t know if that counts as unfinished or just… not the same task anymore.

So I guess I don’t have a clean answer. I can let some things be incomplete-looking, maybe, but I also lose track of what “complete” was supposed to mean in the first place.
Do you feel like you're trying to perfect things when you get caught up in details, or is it more that you just can't help but notice them?

It’s more that I can’t help but notice them. I don’t think I’m trying to make things perfect, exactly.

I’ll be in the middle of something I’m supposed to stay with—like the actual experiment, or a grant call, or a safety meeting—and then there’s this pump vibration, or a student says something off to the side, or I remember some weird peak from an old spectrum. And then my brain just… goes there. I start chasing it, and hours can disappear.

Meanwhile the thing everyone actually needed from me is just falling apart. That’s why I came in, really. I can’t keep my mind on the main thing anymore.
Do you think your brain gets stuck on these small details because they might be important for the task, or because you just can't stop thinking about them once you've noticed them?

I think it starts because it might be important, at least that’s what my brain tells me. Like, a pump vibration could mean something’s wrong with the setup, or a student’s comment might actually matter, or that odd peak in an old spectrum—those things can be real clues.

But then it doesn’t stop there. Once I notice it, I can’t let it go. I came in because I can’t keep my mind on the actual experiment anymore. I’ll be on a grant call or sitting in a safety meeting, and suddenly I’m chasing one of those little things for hours, and meanwhile the thing everyone actually needed from me is falling apart.
Do you feel like you're getting caught up in these details because you're trying to achieve a perfect outcome, or because you're having trouble ignoring the distractions?

It’s not really perfection, no. I mean, I like things to be right, obviously, but that’s not what it feels like.

It’s more like I can’t ignore something once it catches. I came in because I can’t keep my mind on the actual experiment anymore. I’ll be on a grant call, or in a safety meeting, and I’ll hear a pump vibrating a little strangely, or a student will say something off to the side, or I’ll suddenly remember some odd peak from an old spectrum—and then I’m gone. I’m chasing that thread for hours.

And then the thing everyone actually needed from me is just… falling apart while I’m off with the side thing. So no, I don’t think I’m trying to make it perfect. I think I’m just getting pulled away and I can’t make myself come back.
Do you think your tendency to get caught up in details is driven more by a desire to ensure everything is accurate or by an inability to disregard the small things that catch your attention?

More the second one, I think—the not being able to disregard it. I tell myself it’s about accuracy, because in the lab those tiny things can matter, but honestly it doesn’t stay useful.

Like I came in because I can’t keep my mind on the actual experiment anymore. I’ll be on a grant call or in a safety meeting, and there’s a pump vibration, or a student says something off to the side, or I remember some odd peak from an old spectrum—actually, there was one like that in grad school that turned out to be contamination, so my brain treats all of them like emergencies—and then I’m just gone. I’ll chase it for hours.

And meanwhile the thing people needed from me, the main thing, is falling apart. So… yes, accuracy starts it maybe, but I can’t let the small thing go.
Do you think you could function effectively in a setting where things are not perfectly organized or structured?

Not very well right now, no. I mean, the lab is never perfectly organized—there’s always someone moving tubing, a pump making a new sound, somebody talking in the corner—and normally I could work around that.

But lately I can’t. I came in because I can’t keep my mind on the actual experiment anymore. I’ll be in the middle of a grant call or a safety meeting and notice something tiny, like a vibration from a pump, or a student’s side comment, or I’ll remember some weird peak from an old spectrum, and then I’m just off following that for hours.

And it’s not even that the room is messy exactly—sorry, I’m drifting. It’s more that if things aren’t structured enough to keep me locked onto the main task, I get pulled away, and then the thing everyone actually needs from me starts falling apart.
Do you think you get caught up in details because you want to understand them fully or because you cannot help but notice them?

I think it’s more that I can’t help noticing them. I mean, I tell myself I’m trying to understand the whole picture, because in science you’re supposed to notice anomalies, right? That’s how you find things. But lately it’s not… productive like that.

I came in because I can’t keep my mind on the actual experiment anymore. I’ll be on a grant call or in a safety meeting, and there’ll be this pump vibration, or a student will make some side comment, or I’ll suddenly remember an odd peak from an old spectrum, and then that’s all I can think about. I go chasing it for hours.

And meanwhile the actual thing people needed from me is just falling apart. So, no, it’s not really curiosity in a useful way. It’s like the detail grabs me and I can’t not follow it.
